claims.evidence: This claim is supported by QuSAGE pathway analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway in non-lesional DLE skin.
claims.source: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway, with upregulation of a number of IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 and IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 in non-lesional skin (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 are upregulated in non-lesional DLE skin.
claims.source: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway, with upregulation of a number of IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 and IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 in non-lesional skin (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 are upregulated in non-lesional DLE skin.
claims.source: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway, with upregulation of a number of IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 and IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 in non-lesional skin (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The IFN response was overall less dramatic in non-lesional skin compared to lesional skin.
claims.source: Comparison of non-lesional skin with lesional skin showed that this IFN response was overall less dramatic in non-lesional skin (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with findings of previous studies (Billi et al., 2022; Martínez et al., 2022; Psarras et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: ADAR, IRF6, and PTPN1 were expressed at higher levels in non-lesional skin compared to lesional skin.
claims.source: The more muted response did not apply to every gene in the pathway, however, with ADAR, IRF6, and PTPN1 expressed at higher levels in non-lesional skin (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and suggesting a distinct biology in non-lesional and lesional skin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Non-lesional and lesional skin have distinct biology.
claims.source: The more muted response did not apply to every gene in the pathway, however, with ADAR, IRF6, and PTPN1 expressed at higher levels in non-lesional skin (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and suggesting a distinct biology in non-lesional and lesional skin.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential gene expression patterns between non-lesional and lesional skin.

claims.claim: Lesional DLE samples were enriched for immune cell gene sets including plasma cells, T cells, monocyte/myeloid cells, neutrophils, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells when compared to controls.
claims.source: Reanalysis of the lesional skin here reiterated the GSVA results of multiple datasets (Martínez et al., 2022), showing enrichment of immune cell gene sets including plasma cells, T cells, monocyte/myeloid cells, neutrophils, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) when compared to controls (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The LC gene set was de-enriched in lesional DLE skin.
claims.source: The LC gene set was de-enriched in lesional skin, echoing the LC loss seen in other studies (Billi et al., 2022; Bos et al., 1986; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982), and this effect was more dramatic than the LC de-enrichment in lesional psoriatic skin (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: LC de-enrichment in lesional DLE skin was more dramatic than the LC de-enrichment in lesional psoriatic skin.
claims.source: The LC gene set was de-enriched in lesional skin, echoing the LC loss seen in other studies (Billi et al., 2022; Bos et al., 1986; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982), and this effect was more dramatic than the LC de-enrichment in lesional psoriatic skin (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Lesional DLE samples were enriched for inflammatory cytokine gene sets, including IL12, IL21, IL23, TNF, and a highly upregulated IFN gene signature.
claims.source: Lesional DLE samples were also enriched for inflammatory cytokine gene sets, including IL12, IL21, IL23, TNF, and a highly upregulated IFN gene signature as previously seen (Figure 1E; Martínez et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The upregulation of IFN response genes in lesional DLE skin extended to gene signatures indicative of response to specific IFNs, including IFN-Is (IFN-α, β, κ, and ω) and type II IFNs (IFN-γ).
claims.source: The upregulation of IFN response genes in lesional DLE skin extended to gene signatures indicative of response to specific IFNs, including IFN-Is (IFN-α, β, κ, and ω) and type II IFNs (IFN-γ; Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The IFN-γ signature in lesional DLE skin is consistent with the Th1 signature identified in the original study.
claims.source: The IFN-γ signature is consistent with the Th1 signature identified in the original study examining these gene expression data along with cellular phenotyping (Jabbari et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original study.

claims.claim: Non-lesional DLE skin showed upregulation of the IFN gene set when compared to healthy controls, although this change was more modest than in lesional skin.
claims.source: Non-lesional skin also showed upregulation of the IFN gene set in GSVA when compared to healthy controls, although this change was more modest than in lesional skin (Figure 1E–G), similar to that seen in the QuSAGE analysis (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1E-G.

claims.claim: IFN gene set changes in non-lesional DLE skin were driven by IFN-α, IFN-κ, and IFN-ω gene set upregulation.
claims.source: IFN gene set changes in non-lesional skin were driven by IFN-α, IFN-κ, and IFN-ω gene set upregulation (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Non-lesional DLE skin showed de-enrichment of the LC gene set, and this effect was more modest than in lesional skin.
claims.source: Non-lesional skin showed de-enrichment of the LC gene set and this effect was more modest than in lesional skin (Figure 1E and G), consistent with the noticeable loss of LCs in lesional skin compared to adjacent non-lesional skin by immunostaining of tissue sections (Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1E and G, and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Non-lesional DLE skin showed de-enrichment of the keratinocyte gene set, an effect not seen in lesional skin.
claims.source: In contrast, non-lesional skin showed de-enrichment of the keratinocyte gene set, an effect not seen in lesional skin (Figure 1E and G), suggesting a distinct biology in non-lesional and lesional skin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1E and G.

claims.claim: The MRL/lpr model has a Fas gene mutation and develops a lupus-like phenotype especially well on the MRL genetic background.
claims.source: The photosensitive MRL/lpr model has a Fas gene mutation and develops a lupus-like phenotype especially well on the MRL genetic background (Menke et al., 2008; Theofilopoulos and Dixon, 1985).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: MRL/lpr mice have reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and LC Adam17 mRNA.
claims.source: MRL/lpr mice have reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and LC Adam17 mRNA, and topical EGFR ligand supplementation ameliorated photosensitivity (Shipman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Topical EGFR ligand supplementation ameliorated photosensitivity in MRL/lpr mice.
claims.source: MRL/lpr mice have reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and LC Adam17 mRNA, and topical EGFR ligand supplementation ameliorated photosensitivity (Shipman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The IFN-α/β and IFN-γ pathways were among the most highly expressed in MRL/lpr mice compared to control MRL/+ mice.
claims.source: QuSAGE pathway analysis showed that the IFN-α/β and IFN-γ pathways were among the most highly expressed in MRL/lpr mice compared to control MRL/+mice (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by QuSAGE pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: IRF 1, 2, 7, and 9 transcription factors and a number of their targets were expressed at higher levels in MRL/lpr mice.
claims.source: Consistent with the activation of IFN pathways, IRF 1, 2, 7, and 9 transcription factors and a number of their targets were expressed at higher levels in MRL/lpr mice (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The B6.Sle1yaa lupus model is driven by the Sle1 lupus susceptibility locus derived from lupus-prone NZB2410 mice in combination with the Y chromosome autoimmune accelerator locus whose effects are attributed to Tlr7 duplication.
claims.source: The B6.Sle1yaa lupus model is driven by the Sle1 lupus susceptibility locus derived from lupus-prone NZB2410 mice in combination with the Y chromosome autoimmune accelerator locus whose effects are attributed to Tlr7 duplication (Pisitkun et al., 2006; Subramanian et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: B6.Sle1yaa mice are photosensitive and have reduced LC Adam17 mRNA expression.
claims.source: B6.Sle1yaa mice are photosensitive and have reduced LC Adam17 mRNA expression (Shipman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: B6.Sle1yaa mice expressed elevated levels of several lupus related genes from the Yaa locus including Tlr7.
claims.source: As expected, compared to B6 controls, B6.Sle1yaa mice expressed elevated levels of several lupus related genes from the Yaa locus including Tlr7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Several genes involved in the regulation of and response to IFN were expressed at higher levels in B6.Sle1yaa mice, including Irf7, Irf9, Isg15, Xaf1, Selp, and Ube2l6.
claims.source: Although differences between the B6 and B6.Sle1yaa transcriptomes were modest (Figure 2E; Supplementary file 6), several genes involved in the regulation of and response to IFN were expressed at higher levels, including Irf7, Irf9, Isg15, Xaf1, Selp, and Ube2l6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: LC numbers as a proportion of total cells were not different in B6.Sle1yaa mice at 10 months of age when this model is fully diseased.
claims.source: LC numbers as a proportion of total cells were not different at 10 months of age when this model is fully diseased (Shipman et al., 2018), but Cd207 expression was downregulated in these younger (5 month old) diseased mice when compared to B6 controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), potentially hinting at either reduced LC numbers at this time point or altered CD207 expression on LCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Cd207 expression was downregulated in 5 month old B6.Sle1yaa mice when compared to B6 controls.
claims.source: LC numbers as a proportion of total cells were not different at 10 months of age when this model is fully diseased (Shipman et al., 2018), but Cd207 expression was downregulated in these younger (5 month old) diseased mice when compared to B6 controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), potentially hinting at either reduced LC numbers at this time point or altered CD207 expression on LCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The IMQ model is induced by 4–5 weeks of topical IMQ, a TLR 7/8 agonist, resulting in autoantibody production, enlarged spleen and lymph nodes, nephritis, and photosensitivity characteristic of SLE.
claims.source: The IMQ model is induced by 4–5 weeks of topical IMQ, a TLR 7/8 agonist, resulting in autoantibody production, enlarged spleen and lymph nodes, nephritis, and photosensitivity characteristic of SLE (Ambler et al., 2022; Goel et al., 2020; Yokogawa et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The contralateral ear in IMQ mice demonstrated an IFN-I signature, with upregulation of a number of ISGs and IRF 7 and 9.
claims.source: Similar to non-lesional skin in the MRL/lpr mice, the contralateral ear in IMQ mice demonstrated an IFN-I signature, with upregulation of a number of ISGs and IRF 7 and 9 (Figure 2F–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 7, Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2F-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: IFN gamma pathways were not upregulated in IMQ mice, in contrast to MRL/lpr mice.
claims.source: In contrast to MRL/lpr mice, IFN gamma pathways were not upregulated in IMQ mice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of pathway analysis results between MRL/lpr and IMQ mice.

claims.claim: MRL/lpr mice showed increased enrichment of a number of inflammatory cell and cytokine gene sets including T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs, IFN, IL1, IL21, and TNF.
claims.source: By GSVA using lupus-relevant murine gene sets (Supplementary file 9), MRL/lpr mice showed increased enrichment of a number of inflammatory cell and cytokine gene sets including T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs, IFN, IL1, IL21, and TNF (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The keratinocyte signature was enriched in MRL/lpr mice, in contrast to the de-enrichment of this gene set in human DLE.
claims.source: The keratinocyte signature was enriched in MRL/lpr mice, in contrast to the de-enrichment of this gene set in human DLE (Figure 1G, Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1G and 3A.

claims.claim: The LC signature did not show any quantitative changes in MRL/lpr mice, consistent with unchanged LC numbers in the skin of MRL/lpr mice.
claims.source: The LC signature did not show any quantitative changes; assuming that this gene set could in part reflect LC numbers, this result was consistent with unchanged LC numbers in the skin of MRL/lpr mice (Shipman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The IFN gene set upregulation in MRL/lpr non-lesional skin was broad, with significant enrichment of gene signatures induced by stimulation from multiple IFNs.
claims.source: Similar to human DLE, the IFN gene set upregulation in MRL/lpr non-lesional skin was broad, with significant enrichment of gene signatures induced by stimulation from multiple IFNs (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: B6.Sle1yaa mice showed upregulation of the IFN gene set without a particular contribution from any one IFN.
claims.source: B6.Sle1yaa mice showed less dramatic differences than the MRL/lpr model, but also showed upregulation of the IFN gene set without a particular contribution from any one IFN (Figure 3C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 3C-D.

claims.claim: The LC gene set was de-enriched in B6.Sle1yaa mice.
claims.source: The LC gene set was de-enriched in B6.Sle1yaa mice (Figure 3C), driven in part by the reduction in Cd207 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), potentially reflecting decreased LC numbers or altered LC phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3C and gene expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The contralateral 'non-lesional' ears from IMQ-treated mice exhibited significant upregulation of the IFN gene signature and were similar to MRL/lpr mice in showing enriched gene signatures of myeloid cells, IL21, and TNF.
claims.source: The contralateral 'non-lesional' ears from IMQ-treated mice also exhibited significant upregulation of the IFN gene signature and were similar to MRL/lpr mice in showing enriched gene signatures of myeloid cells, IL21, and TNF (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: T cell genes were uniquely de-enriched in IMQ skin.
claims.source: T cell genes were uniquely de-enriched in IMQ skin (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The LC gene set was not altered in non-lesional IMQ skin.
claims.source: The LC gene set was not altered (Figure 3E), although there was de-enrichment in IMQ-painted ipsilateral skin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The IFN signature in non-lesional IMQ skin reflected enrichment of multiple IFN-I gene sets.
claims.source: Similar to human DLE and MRL/lpr mice, the IFN signature in non-lesional IMQ skin reflected enrichment of multiple IFN-I gene sets (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The overall IFN gene set was not enriched in the IMQ-painted ipsilateral skin.
claims.source: Interestingly, the overall IFN gene set was not enriched in the IMQ-painted ipsilateral skin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although there was enrichment in two of the specific IFN signatures (IFNB1 and IFNW1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: All genes common to human DLE, MRL/lpr, and IMQ datasets (Sprr1b, Isg15, Ddx60, Bst2, Xaf1, Rsad2, Slc7a8, Ifit3) were interferon-inducible genes.
claims.source: All of these genes (Sprr1b, Isg15, Ddx60, Bst2, Xaf1, Rsad2, Slc7a8, Ifit3) were interferon-inducible genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of overlapping differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In pairwise set overlaps (DLE – MRL/lpr, MRL/lpr – IMQ or IMQ – MRL/lpr) large proportion of overlapping genes were IFN-inducible targets including Ifi genes (Ifi44, 203, 204), IRF transcription factors (Irf 1,2,7, 8, and 9), Oas 2,3 and L2, Mx1.
claims.source: Similarly, in pairwise set overlaps (DLE – MRL/lpr, MRL/lpr – IMQ or IMQ – MRL/lpr) large proportion of overlapping genes were IFN-inducible targets including Ifi genes (Ifi44, 203, 204), IRF transcription factors (Irf 1,2,7, 8, and 9), Oas 2,3 and L2, Mx1 (Supplementary file 10).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of overlapping differentially expressed genes.

claims.claim: IFN upregulation correlated with loss of LCs in human DLE and B6.Sle1yaa mice but not in MRL/lpr and IMQ mice.
claims.source: Notably, IFN upregulation correlated with loss of LCs in human DLE and B6.Sle1yaa mice but not in MRL/lpr and IMQ mice (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of GSVA scores shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The lack of correlation between IFN upregulation and LC loss in IMQ mice extended to the painted ipsilateral ear, where there was a reduced LC signature in the absence of IFN upregulation.
claims.source: The lack of correlation in IMQ mice also extended to the painted ipsilateral ear, where there was a reduced LC signature in the absence of IFN upregulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: UVR treatment of a mixture of digested epidermal cells induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss.
claims.source: As we had studied LC ADAM17 sheddase activity using isolated LCs, we confirmed here that UVR treatment of a mixture of digested epidermal cells also induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: UVR-induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss is LC ADAM17-dependent.
claims.source: This effect was LC ADAM17-dependent (Figure 5A), validating UVR-induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss as a readout of LC ADAM17 activity in the context of a mixture of epidermal cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A comparing WT and LCAd17 mice.

claims.claim: IFN-κ reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase activity by nearly 40% when used to treat LCs ex vivo.
claims.source: IFN-κ, an IFN-I that is highly expressed by lupus keratinocytes (Tsoi et al., 2019), reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase activity by nearly 40% when used to treat LCs ex vivo (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: IFN-κ reduced LC ADAM17 protein levels only modestly by 8% and had no effect on cell viability.
claims.source: In contrast, IFN-κ reduced LC ADAM17 protein levels only modestly by 8% and had no effect on cell viability (Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D-E.

claims.claim: The IFN-κ-driven inhibition of ADAM17 activity was abrogated by the JAK1/3 inhibitor tofacitinib.
claims.source: The IFN-κ-driven inhibition of ADAM17 activity was abrogated by the JAK1/3 inhibitor tofacitinib (Figure 5F) without altering ADAM17 protein levels (Figure 5G) or cell viability (Figure 5H), supporting the idea that IFN-κ mainly affected LC ADAM17 by inhibiting sheddase activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5F-H.

claims.claim: IFN-β reduced LC ADAM17 activity without effects on cell viability ex vivo.
claims.source: Another IFN-I, IFN-β, similarly reduced LC ADAM17 activity without effects on cell viability ex vivo (Figure 5I–J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5I-J.

claims.claim: In vivo application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced LC ADAM17-mediated shedding by 57%.
claims.source: In vivo, application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced LC ADAM17-mediated shedding by 57% (Figure 5K) while cell surface ADAM17 was reduced by 9% (Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5K-L.

claims.claim: In vivo application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced cell surface ADAM17 by 9%.
claims.source: In vivo, application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced LC ADAM17-mediated shedding by 57% (Figure 5K) while cell surface ADAM17 was reduced by 9% (Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L.

claims.claim: In vivo application of IFN-κ had no effect on LC numbers.
claims.source: There was no effect on LC numbers (Figure 5M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M.

claims.claim: IFN-β reduced human LC ADAM17 activity by 62% without altering ADAM17 expression or LC viability.
claims.source: Addition of IFN-β reduced LC ADAM17 activity by 62% without altering ADAM17 expression or LC viability (Figure 5N–P).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5N-P.

claims.claim: MRL/lpr mice showed a 42% reduction in LC ADAM17 sheddase activity when compared to control MRL/+ mice.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings (Shipman et al., 2018), MRL/lpr mice showed a 42% reduction in LC ADAM17 sheddase activity when compared to control MRL/+mice (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: LC ADAM17 protein levels in MRL/lpr mice showed a 21% reduction compared to controls.
claims.source: LC ADAM17 protein levels, however, were less affected, showing a 21% reduction (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Intraperitoneal anti-IFNAR treatment of MRL/lpr mice at 500 μg/dose restored UVR-induced LC TNFR1 loss.
claims.source: Intraperitoneal (i.p.) anti-IFNAR treatment of MRL/lpr mice at 500 μg/dose restored UVR-induced LC TNFR1 loss (Figure 6A), suggesting restoration of LC ADAM17 sheddase activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Anti-IFNAR at 500 μg/dose did not alter cell surface ADAM17 protein expression in MRL/lpr mice.
claims.source: Anti-IFNAR did not alter cell surface ADAM17 protein expression (Figure 6B), suggesting that IFN-I regulated LC ADAM17 sheddase function rather than expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: A lower 125 μg/dose of anti-IFNAR had similar effects in restoring LC ADAM17 sheddase activity without affecting LC ADAM17 protein levels in MRL/lpr mice.
claims.source: A lower 125 μg/dose of anti-IFNAR had similar effects in restoring LC ADAM17 sheddase activity without affecting LC ADAM17 protein levels (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claims.claim: LCs from the B6.Sle1yaa model showed a 63% reduction in UVR-induced TNFR1 loss when compared to control B6 mice without a corresponding change in cell surface ADAM17 protein levels.
claims.source: LCs from the B6.Sle1yaa model showed a 63% reduction in UVR-induced TNFR1 loss when compared to control B6 mice without a corresponding change in cell surface ADAM17 protein levels (Figure 6E–F), suggesting reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function in this SLE model.

results.result: Non-lesional skin from human lupus (DLE) and three murine lupus models (MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, IMQ) share an IFN-rich environment characterized by upregulation of IFN-I pathways, IFN-stimulated genes, and IRF transcription factors, though the magnitude and specific features vary across models.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C73 collectively demonstrate through transcriptomic analysis (microarray and RNAseq) that non-lesional skin across human DLE and three murine models exhibits IFN signatures. The data include QuSAGE pathway analysis, GSVA, and differential gene expression showing consistent upregulation of IFN-I pathways and ISGs. The findings are supported by multiple figures (1-4) showing PCA, volcano plots, heatmaps, and pathway enrichment analyses with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR<0.05).

results.result: Lesional DLE skin shows enrichment of immune cell gene sets (plasma cells, T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs), inflammatory cytokine signatures (IL12, IL21, IL23, TNF, IFN), and dramatic LC gene set de-enrichment compared to controls and psoriatic skin.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E-F with appropriate statistical testing. The findings are consistent with cited previous studies and the original study characterizing these samples. The LC de-enrichment is more dramatic than in psoriatic skin, providing a disease-specific comparison.

results.result: MRL/lpr mice show enrichment of inflammatory cell and cytokine gene sets including T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs, IFN, IL1, IL21, and TNF, with enriched keratinocyte signature but unchanged LC signature.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by GSVA analysis in Figure 3A using lupus-relevant murine gene sets. The unchanged LC signature is consistent with previous findings (Shipman et al., 2018) showing unchanged LC numbers in MRL/lpr mice, providing internal consistency.

results.result: IFN-I (IFN-κ and IFN-β) inhibits LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in both murine and human LCs ex vivo and in vivo, with minimal effects on ADAM17 protein expression or LC numbers, and this inhibition is JAK1/3-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C74-C83 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing dose-dependent reduction in UVR-induced TNFR1 loss (sheddase activity readout) with IFN-κ (~40% reduction ex vivo, 57% in vivo) and IFN-β (62% in human LCs). The assay was validated using LCAd17 mice (C74-C75). Effects on ADAM17 protein were modest (8-9%) and LC numbers unchanged. Tofacitinib abrogated the effect, confirming JAK-dependence. Sample sizes (n=3-10) and statistical tests (paired/unpaired t-tests) are appropriate.

results.result: IFNAR blockade restores LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in three lupus models (MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, IMQ) without consistent effects on ADAM17 protein expression or LC numbers, demonstrating that IFN-I specifically regulates sheddase function.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C84-C95 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and Table 1 showing that anti-IFNAR treatment restored LC ADAM17 sheddase activity across all three models (42-63% reduction in disease, restored by anti-IFNAR) without consistently affecting protein levels or LC numbers. The consistency across models and the uncoupling of activity from expression/cell numbers (Table 1) strongly support the conclusion. Sample sizes (n=3-9) and statistical methods are appropriate.

results.result: Anti-IFNAR-mediated restoration of LC ADAM17 sheddase function reduces photosensitive responses (ear swelling, epidermal permeability, inflammatory infiltrates) in lupus mice, and this effect is dependent on EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C96-C108 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing that anti-IFNAR at 125 μg/dose reduced UVR-induced ear swelling, epidermal permeability, and neutrophil/monocyte infiltration in MRL/lpr and IMQ mice. The EGFR inhibitor PD168393 abrogated these effects (C104), and anti-IFNAR failed to reduce monocyte accumulation in LCAd17 mice lacking LC ADAM17 (C108), demonstrating dependence on EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17. The dose-response findings (C96-C101) showing that high-dose anti-IFNAR increased photosensitivity in control mice are consistent with cited literature on IFNAR deficiency effects.

results.result: UVR-induced LC ROS production is reduced in lupus model mice, restored by anti-IFNAR treatment, and is predominantly cytoplasmic in origin.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C109-C111 are supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing reduced UVR-induced ROS in IMQ mice, restoration by anti-IFNAR, and cytoplasmic (CellROX) rather than mitochondrial (MitoSOX) origin. Sample sizes (n=5-6) and statistical tests are appropriate. This provides a mechanistic link between IFN-I and ADAM17 activity, as ROS is a known mediator of ADAM17 function.

results.result: IFN-I promotes photosensitivity at least in part by inhibiting UVR-induced LC ADAM17 sheddase function, likely through reduction of LC ROS generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C113, C125 represent the main mechanistic conclusion integrating the experimental findings. This is supported by the convergence of evidence showing: (1) IFN-I inhibits LC ADAM17 activity, (2) anti-IFNAR restores activity, (3) anti-IFNAR reduces photosensitivity in an EGFR- and LC ADAM17-dependent manner, and (4) IFN-I reduces ROS, a known ADAM17 activator. The inference is well-supported by the data, though the authors appropriately use cautious language ('at least in part', 'suggest').

results.result: Anifrolumab may ameliorate lupus skin disease in part by restoring LC ADAM17 sheddase function, and IFNAR blockade should prevent new lesion formation and treat existing lesions if physiologic IFN levels are preserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C122 are speculative extrapolations from the mouse data to human therapeutic implications. While the mouse experiments with anti-IFNAR support the mechanism, direct evidence that anifrolumab works through this mechanism in human patients is not provided. The authors appropriately frame these as possibilities ('raise the possibility', 'should'), but clinical validation would be needed to support these claims.

results.result: The shared pathogenic mechanisms across murine models and human lupus, particularly LC ADAM17 sheddase dysfunction, establish these models as useful for studying lupus skin pathophysiology and identify LC ADAM17 function as a therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C126, C129 are supported by the consistent findings across human DLE and three murine models showing IFN signatures and LC ADAM17 dysfunction. The uncoupling of sheddase activity from protein expression and cell numbers (Table 1) across all models and interventions strongly supports LC ADAM17 function as a key contributor. The inference about model utility is reasonable given the shared mechanisms demonstrated.

results.result: A proposed pathogenic model suggests keratinocyte-derived IFN-I causes LC ADAM17 dysfunction, creating a feed-forward loop leading to keratinocyte damage and lesion formation, with distinct IFN functions in non-lesional (priming) versus lesional (damage) skin.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C121 represent a speculative disease model integrating the findings with spatial biology considerations. While the model is consistent with the data (keratinocytes express IFN, LCs are nearby, IFN inhibits LC ADAM17), direct evidence for the feed-forward loop and the proposed distinct functions in non-lesional versus lesional skin is limited. The model is plausible but requires additional experimental validation, particularly regarding keratinocyte-LC interactions and the progression from non-lesional to lesional skin.

results.result: LC loss is a feature of human lupus skin that is variable in non-lesional skin and more consistent in lesional skin, while LC numbers appear less affected in lupus mouse models.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C133 are supported by GSVA analysis of LC gene sets in this manuscript and multiple cited studies. The variability in non-lesional skin and consistency in lesional skin are documented across multiple studies. The comparison between human and mouse models is appropriately cautious, noting that mouse models show less dramatic LC loss. This provides important context for interpreting the model systems.

results.result: Background on lupus photosensitivity and prior findings that LCs limit photosensitivity via ADAM17-mediated EGFR ligand release, with reduced LC ADAM17 activity in lupus models and patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C13-C18 represent background information and prior work, primarily from Shipman et al., 2018. These are well-established facts (C1, C13, C14) or findings from the authors' previous work (C2, C3, C15-C18) that provide context for the current study. The claims are appropriately cited and provide the rationale for investigating IFN-I effects on LC ADAM17.

results.result: Background on IFN signatures in lupus tissues and blood, the importance of IFN-I in disease pathogenesis highlighted by anifrolumab approval, and the IFN-rich environment in non-lesional skin.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C26 represent well-established background information supported by multiple citations to published studies and regulatory approval of anifrolumab. These provide the scientific context and rationale for investigating IFN-I effects on LC function in lupus skin. The claims are appropriately cited and establish the importance of IFN-I in lupus pathogenesis.

results.result: Characterization of the three murine lupus models (MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, IMQ) including their genetic basis, disease features, and previous findings of LC ADAM17 dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C56 provide background on the three murine models used in the study. The characterizations are supported by citations to published studies (C45, C50, C56) and the authors' previous work (C46, C47, C51, C54). The new RNAseq data (C52, C53, C55) are appropriately presented with figures. This establishes the models as relevant for studying lupus skin pathophysiology.

results.result: Background on IFN-I functions in normal skin physiology, ADAM17 biology in other contexts, and IFN-I states in other diseases, providing broader context for the findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C99, C100, C117, C123, C124, C127, C134-C137 provide broader biological context from published literature. These are appropriately cited and help interpret the findings in the context of normal physiology (IFN-I in wound healing, ADAM17 regulation) and other diseases (interferonopathies, dermatomyositis, checkpoint inhibitor toxicity). This contextualizes the specific findings in lupus.

results.result: Speculation that modulating ADAM17 enzymatic function offers advantages over controlling transcription/translation or LC numbers for regulating UVR responses.
results.evaluation: Claim C128 is explicitly speculative ('We speculate') about the biological advantages of regulating enzyme activity versus expression or cell numbers. While the speculation is reasonable given the data showing uncoupling of activity from expression/numbers, it lacks direct experimental support. The authors appropriately frame this as speculation.
